picks.flagship: Rittenhouse Straight Rye Whisky Bottled in Bond
picks.why: A Philadelphia rye name, first sold by Continental Distilling, that Heaven Hill took over in 1993 and has made in Kentucky since. The bonded bottling is the one to know: four years old, 100 proof, from a mash at the legal minimum of 51 per cent rye, which is the Kentucky way with rye and the bar's working rye for a Manhattan or a Sazerac.
picks.note: Sources differ on the mash: 51 rye, 35 corn, 14 malted barley on Heaven Hill linked sheets, 51, 37, 12 in several reviews; confirm on Heaven Hill's own sheet. Heaven Hill's claim that it follows a Pennsylvania style is disputed; keep it out of the why. The bonded label also fits the bottled-in-bond group in the other American lane; it is placed here because a bartender reaches for it as a rye. Library holds the maker, Heaven Hill, not the label.

picks.why: The Sazerac Company's own rye, named for the New Orleans cocktail and distilled at Buffalo Trace in Frankfort from its low rye mash. Bottled at 90 proof, it is the rye that the Sazerac cocktail is now built on by name.
picks.note: The label carries no age statement; it is widely said to be about six years old and some retail copy still says 6 Year, but this is not on the label: leave it out or give it as a belief. The mash bill is not published. A 100 proof bottling was added in 2025 and an 18 year release exists; neither is the flagship. Library holds the maker, Buffalo Trace.

picks.flagship: Thomas H. Handy Sazerac Straight Rye
picks.why: The rye of the Buffalo Trace Antique Collection, released once a year uncut and unfiltered at barrel proof and named for Thomas H. Handy, the New Orleans bar owner behind the Sazerac Company. It is Sazerac Rye's mash at full strength, the bottle on the owner's own shelf.
picks.note: Proof moves by release (about 126 in 2016, about 130 in 2025). Maxim reports that from the 2026 release every barrel is at least 12 years old, against about six years before; only one source, so confirm on Buffalo Trace's 2026 release before stating an age. It also suits the barrel-proof group in the other American lane; placed here as a rye, and it is a shelf bottle.

picks.why: A Maryland rye name from 1895, made in Maryland until the 1970s and in Kentucky by Heaven Hill since; the six year old 110 proof bottling of 2015 is the one to know. It teaches how a Maryland name came to stand for a Kentucky rye.
picks.note: Sources disagree on when Heaven Hill took the brand (1982 in one, the 1980s in Heaven Hill's release) and on the mash (51 rye, 39 corn, 10 barley against 65, 23, 12): confirm on Heaven Hill's sheet. Made at the Bernheim Distillery per one source. The older 80 proof three year Pikesville is still sold in Maryland; do not confuse the two. Could be told under monongahela-rye as history; placed here because the whiskey is Kentucky made, as the benchmarks place it.

picks.flagship: Michter's US*1 Single Barrel Kentucky Straight Rye
picks.why: A Louisville house whose name goes back to a Pennsylvania distillery, and whose US*1 rye is bottled one barrel at a time at 84.8 proof. It is the rye a guest asks for by the Michter's name, gentler in proof than the bonded ryes.
picks.note: Michter's also sells a US*1 bourbon; if the other American lane claims Michter's as a bourbon label, drop this pick for an alternate. Sources differ on where it is distilled (Shively or Fort Nelson in Louisville, and older reviews call it sourced): say Louisville, Kentucky only until Michter's own page settles it. Mash bill (53, 33, 14 per one retailer) unconfirmed. Library name carries a curly apostrophe: Michter’s.

alternates.why: A historic Kentucky name revived in Lexington, distilling again on its own site since December 2017; the 1776 rye is bottled at 100 proof. Note: one source calls it 100 per cent rye, which is not a Kentucky-style low rye mash, so check before using it here.
The benchmarks name Wild Turkey for this style. Not searched in this run, and Wild Turkey is first a bourbon label, so it stands only if the other lane does not use it.

picks.why: The Overholt family's rye from West Overton in Pennsylvania, first distilled in 1810, and the name that carries the Monongahela story to the bar. Today it is a four year old straight rye at 86 proof, made in Kentucky.
picks.note: Tell the Pennsylvania distilling as history in the past tense: Beam bought the brand in 1987 and moved production to Kentucky (1987 or 1993 by source); it is now made at Clermont, Kentucky. The 2019 change to 43 per cent, no chill filtering and four years is from one source; confirm. A bonded bottling from 2018 exists. Library holds the maker as Jim Beam.

picks.why: The Baltimore distillery that brought Maryland rye back to the bar. Its Signature Rye blends two straight rye mash bills, one high in rye for spice and one lower for sweetness, at 83 proof.
picks.note: Sources say earlier batches were sourced from MGP in Indiana and the Bottled in Bond was its first fully own made rye; confirm what the current Signature batch is before calling it Maryland distilled. Age given as four to six years by the distillery, two years by one source. Founding year not confirmed in this run.

picks.why: A family owned distillery in Pittsburgh's Strip District that set out to revive Monongahela rye, grain to glass from regional organic rye. Its straight rye is the bottling that shows the western Pennsylvania style at the bar.
picks.note: No source settled a single core bottling or its proof (47.2, 50.5 and 100 proof listed for different rye bottlings; a single barrel rye at 68 rye, 18 wheat, 14 barley). Confirm the current core rye and its label name on Wigle's own site. Founding year not confirmed (2011 assumed, not found). Corporate name differs between sources.

picks.why: Made in Bristol, Pennsylvania, since 2011 from a mash of 80 per cent rye with malted barley and malted rye and no corn, in the pure rye way of old Monongahela. The classic bottling, aged in quarter casks and bottled at 90 proof, is the one to know.
picks.note: A living co founder is named in the press; keep him out of prose. Latest confirmation it is operating is a 2024 profile; check it is still open. The bonded bottling is listed at 95 and 100 proof by different sellers; bonded must be 100, so confirm. The classic's age (about eight and a half months in quarter casks) is from one older source.

picks.why: A Washington, Pennsylvania distillery carrying the old Monongahela tradition forward with a high rye mash. Its Old Monongahela rye, bottled at its 108 barrel entry proof, puts the style's name on the label.
picks.note: Introduced in 2024 and sold in batches, so proof may move; a 92 proof straight rye is also made and may suit as the everyday flagship: author to choose. Some reviews misspell the maker as Mango Creek. Not on the benchmarks list.

alternates.why: A Lititz, Pennsylvania distillery that began as a revival of the Bomberger's name near Schaefferstown and changed name after a dispute with Michter's; its rye is a 65 rye, 25 corn, 10 malt mash at 45 per cent. Opening year differs by source; its distiller is living, keep him out of prose.
A Baltimore distillery whose Epoch Rye of 2018 was the first rye distilled in the city in over fifty years, from 70 per cent rye grain and 30 per cent rye malt, a nod to the sweeter Maryland style.

picks.why: A Seattle distillery founded in 2010 whose American Oak, first released in 2013, is its flagship: malted barley aged in new charred American oak and bottled at 46 per cent. It is the bottle that shows what the new category tastes like.
picks.note: Maturation differs by source (at least 24 months against 40 months for another Westland malt). Its parent company was not confirmed in this run; leave ownership out.

picks.flagship: Stranahan's Original American Single Malt Whiskey
picks.why: A Denver distillery founded in 2004 whose Original, first bottled in 2006, is aged at least four years in new charred oak and bottled at 94 proof. It is the Colorado malt a guest asks for by name.
picks.note: Owned by Proximo since 2010 per one directory; a blend of six to nine year malts per the same directory against the brand's four year minimum: use the brand's figure. Older labels read Stranahan's Colorado Whiskey; confirm the label name today.

picks.why: Clear Creek's peated malt from Oregon, first distilled in 1991 and released in 1996 by its founder Steve McCarthy, years before American single malt was a term. It teaches where the category came from.
picks.note: Steve McCarthy has died, so he may be named. Clear Creek was sold to Hood River Distillers in 2014. Current bottling (a six year release is listed) and proof not confirmed in this run.

picks.why: A Portland, Oregon malt brewed and distilled from Northwest two row barley and aged in new, lightly charred American oak, bottled at 90 proof. It is the original Westward bottling, with stout cask and cask strength versions beside it.
picks.note: Its master distiller is living; keep him out of prose. Ownership not confirmed (no source named Diageo); leave it out.

picks.flagship: Courage & Conviction American Single Malt Whisky
picks.why: A Lovingston, Virginia distillery given over to single malt, whose flagship of 2020 is distilled on site from North American malted barley, aged at least three years and bottled at 46 per cent. It shows the category reaching the East.
picks.note: One source calls it the largest dedicated American single malt distillery; keep that out. Its founder is described as Dr. George G. Moore; check whether he is living before naming him. The label may read Signature Malt in recent releases; confirm the current name.

alternates.why: A Seattle distillery that brews its own beer for its malt and numbers every release; its PeatSmith releases use Washington barley and Washington peat.
Waco's malt from Texas grown barley alongside Golden Promise. Balcones is a pick in corn-whiskey in this lane, so this stands only if that pick moves.

picks.flagship: Mellow Corn Bottled in Bond Kentucky Straight Corn Whiskey
picks.why: Heaven Hill's corn whiskey, bonded: at least four years in a bonded warehouse and 100 proof, from a mash of about 90 per cent corn. It is the aged corn whiskey a bar carries, and the clearest bottle for the rule that corn whiskey goes into used or uncharred oak.
picks.note: The used or uncharred oak rule is the style's own, from the Cask Atlas; not searched in this run. Mash share from a retailer. Also bonded, but placed here because the lesson is corn.

picks.why: A corn whiskey in a mason jar, made in Kentucky by Heaven Hill from at least 81 per cent corn and bottled at 80 proof, with "less than 30 days old" on its label. It shows the young, near clear end of the style.
picks.note: Some sources call it unaged and the maker's sheet says lightly aged; quote the label's own words. A 100 proof Fruit Jar version exists.

picks.why: A Gatlinburg, Tennessee distillery opened in 2010 whose Original is labelled as Tennessee corn whiskey: unaged, clear and 100 proof from about 80 per cent corn. It is the moonshine a guest names, and it teaches that legal moonshine is corn whiskey with no oak.
picks.note: The licensing milestone is told differently by source (first federally licensed in East Tennessee, or first under the new state law); leave it out or confirm. The legal class on the label (corn whiskey) is from retail label images; confirm on the label itself.

picks.why: A three year old corn whiskey sold in a stoneware jug at 80 proof by McCormick Distilling. It is the jug a guest remembers, and an aged corn beside the young ones.
picks.note: Age given as 36 months by most and 30 months by one seller; the older 100 proof bottling is no longer listed. Where McCormick distils it was not confirmed; say bottled by McCormick unless confirmed.

picks.why: Waco's first whisky, launched in 2009 from roasted heirloom blue corn, distilled twice and aged in small oak barrels, at 92 proof. It shows a craft corn whisky built to be sipped, and it is spelt whisky on the label.
picks.note: First Texas whisky since Prohibition is the brand's own claim; keep it out of the why unless a second source confirms it. The corn began as Hopi blue corn from New Mexico and is now a blue flint corn grown in West Texas.

alternates.why: Piedmont Distillers' North Carolina moonshine made entirely from corn on a family recipe. Note: Difford's lists it as a corn vodka, so confirm its legal class before using it as corn whiskey.
The Hudson Valley's corn whiskey. Not confirmed in this run that it is made today; check before use.

left.why: A label term, not a kind of producer. Straight qualifies bourbon, rye, wheat and corn whiskey, and the bottlings a bartender is asked for by name carry it as bourbon or rye, not as their identity; no five labels sell themselves as straight whiskey alone. It is taught through the rye, corn and bourbon groups (Rittenhouse, Pikesville, Old Overholt, Mellow Corn all print straight).

Thin. Only three labels a guest would meet are wheat whiskey first: Bernheim Original (Heaven Hill, seven years, 90 proof, 51 wheat, released 2005), Dry Fly (Spokane, Washington wheat) and Middle West. Woodford Reserve Wheat and Old Elk Wheat are real but come from labels that are first bourbon labels, and the Weller and Stitzel-Weller names in the prose are wheated bourbons. Fewer than five, so no group: Bernheim Original is the one bottle to teach the style.

Thin as a style a guest names. Seagram's 7 Crown (Diageo, 80 proof, about 75 per cent neutral grain spirit) and Kessler (founded 1888, Smooth as Silk, now Suntory Global Spirits, 80 proof) are asked for by name; Fleischmann's Preferred (Sazerac Company, 80 proof) is a rail bottle; Imperial and Calvert Extra are still listed but nothing more could be confirmed. High West, on the benchmarks, sells blends of straight whiskeys, not blended American whiskey with neutral spirit, so it is not of the style. No light whiskey label is in general sale. Two real names and three rail blends do not make five a bartender is expected to know; teach Seagram's 7 Crown and Kessler in the style's own prose.
